paragraphs: Total variation models are widely used in signal processing, but solving them becomes difficult as the number of variables grows. The paper targets a computational bottleneck in leading approaches based on the alternating direction method of multipliers: they often require solving large linear systems. That work can make large signal and image problems expensive.

The proposed algorithm divides the problem domain using a new decomposition strategy. This turns the original optimization problem into small, independent subproblems with closed-form solutions. Independence is the key practical feature: separate processes can solve these pieces in parallel, while closed-form solutions simplify the work required for each piece.

The authors prove convergence to a global minimum and give a time complexity of O(N/(ε n_p)) for reaching an ε-optimal solution with N variables and n_p processes. The bound explicitly connects problem size, requested accuracy, and parallel resources. Experiments report better performance than existing leading algorithms, particularly for very large, high-resolution images.
icml-2014-a-highly-scalable-parallel-alg.tldr: A domain decomposition makes total variation optimization parallelizable through small, closed-form subproblems, with global convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: When people judge search quality or consumer satisfaction, their answers often belong to ordered categories. Combining those answers requires handling disagreement among annotators. The paper focuses on a particular structure in that disagreement: workers commonly struggle to distinguish neighboring categories, while categories farther apart are easier to tell apart.

The authors build an aggregation method around this observation. They use minimax conditional entropy with constraints that encode the different difficulty of nearby and distant distinctions. The ordering therefore contributes information to the aggregation procedure. A disagreement between adjacent categories carries a different interpretation from a disagreement spanning a large part of the rating scale.

Evaluations on real datasets show significant improvements over existing methods. These findings support using the geometry of an ordered label scale when combining noisy judgments. The contribution is both a method for producing aggregate labels and a concrete modeling principle: the pattern of likely annotation errors should reflect how workers distinguish the available categories.
icml-2014-aggregating-ordinal-labels-fro.tldr: An ordinal-label aggregation method improves crowd judgments by modeling neighboring categories as harder to distinguish than distant ones.

paragraphs: Anomaly ranking learns a score from unlabeled observations so that the resulting ordering reflects the underlying probability density. The paper evaluates this ordering through the Mass Volume curve, with lower curves representing better performance under its criterion. The challenge is to optimize that curve without being given labels identifying anomalies.

The authors prove an equivalence under the assumption that the data distribution has compact support. In this setting, anomaly ranking becomes a supervised ranking problem that distinguishes observations from the data distribution from observations drawn uniformly over the same support. The Mass Volume curve is then a simple transformation of the corresponding ROC curve.

This connection allows established bipartite ranking algorithms, potentially combined with random sampling, to address Mass Volume minimization. Supervision comes from distinguishing the two distributions rather than from manually labeling anomalies. Numerical experiments using several existing ranking algorithms illustrate the approach's relevance. The compact-support condition is central to the stated equivalence and its interpretation.
icml-2014-anomaly-ranking-as-supervised-.tldr: For distributions with compact support, anomaly ranking can be reformulated as supervised ranking against a uniform reference distribution.

paragraphs: Clustering becomes harder when meaningful groups coexist with an unstructured collection of points. The paper studies how an algorithm can recover the embedded groups despite this background noise. Its focus is on making robustness precise enough to compare methods and prove what they can recover.

The authors introduce quantitative robustness measures that account for both the strength of the cluster structure and how mild the noise is. This ties the desired guarantee to properties of the input. Stronger organization and less disruptive background points provide a different recovery setting from weakly organized data with more troublesome noise.

Using these measures, the paper proposes a simple, efficient procedure for turning any centroid-based clustering algorithm into a noise-robust version. It proves robustness guarantees for the resulting method and shows that more straightforward modifications do not achieve comparable guarantees. The contribution therefore combines a reusable modification with a framework for explaining why seemingly reasonable alternatives can fall short.
icml-2014-clustering-in-the-presence-of-.tldr: The paper gives a general way to make centroid-based clustering robust to background noise, with guarantees tied to cluster strength and noise mildness.

paragraphs: Generative Stochastic Networks introduce a training principle for probabilistic models that offers an alternative to maximum likelihood. The model learns how a Markov chain moves between states, with the aim that its stationary distribution estimates the data distribution. Learning a transition rule becomes the central modeling task.

The motivation is that a conditional distribution describing a small move generally has fewer dominant modes than the full data distribution, becoming unimodal in the small-move limit. This can make the learning problem resemble supervised function approximation, with gradients obtained through backpropagation. The theory extends probabilistic interpretations of denoising autoencoders and gives a joint distribution and sampling mechanism even for inconsistent conditionals.

The framework also supports missing inputs and sampling some variables while holding others fixed. Experiments on two image datasets validate the theoretical results using an architecture resembling a Deep Boltzmann Machine Gibbs sampler. That architecture can be trained by backpropagation without layerwise pretraining, demonstrating how the transition-based formulation connects generative modeling to a familiar training procedure.
icml-2014-deep-generative-stochastic-net.tldr: Generative Stochastic Networks learn Markov-chain transitions by backpropagation so that the chain's stationary distribution estimates the data distribution.

paragraphs: Exchangeability means that permuting a sequence of random variables leaves its joint distribution unchanged. The paper introduces exchangeable variable models, whose building blocks use partial exchangeability, a generalization of this symmetry. This provides a way to construct probabilistic models around distributional structure beyond assumptions that variables are independent.

The authors identify a tractable family of these models and prove that it is optimal under zero-one loss for a broad class of functions, including parity and threshold functions. They also show that this family strictly contains existing tractable model families based on independence. The theoretical result therefore concerns both prediction and the range of structures the models can represent.

Extensive experiments report better performance than leading classifiers such as SVMs and probabilistic models built solely on independence assumptions. These results support partial exchangeability as a useful modeling ingredient. The significance is that richer dependence structure can coexist with tractability, with the optimality claim applying to the function class and loss studied.
icml-2014-exchangeable-variable-models-b.tldr: Exchangeable variable models use partial symmetry to represent dependencies tractably and achieve theoretical and empirical advantages over independence-based models.

paragraphs: Sequential global optimization chooses evaluation points one after another while searching for a function's optimum. This paper studies an algorithmic framework that uses Gaussian processes to guide those choices. Its theoretical focus is cumulative regret, which captures the accumulated shortfall of the chosen evaluations relative to optimal choices.

The authors derive upper bounds for the generic framework that improve previously known bounds for algorithms such as GP-UCB by an exponential factor. This is an improvement in the mathematical performance guarantee. They also introduce Gaussian Process Mutual Information, or GP-MI, and show that it yields a further significant improvement in these cumulative-regret bounds.

Experiments on synthetic and real tasks compare GP-MI with GP-UCB and the Expected Improvement heuristic, supporting the new algorithm's efficiency. The paper thus contributes both a sharper analysis of an existing algorithmic family and a new optimization method. Together, the results connect stronger regret guarantees with evidence of useful performance in the evaluated tasks.
icml-2014-gaussian-process-optimization-.tldr: The paper sharpens Gaussian-process optimization regret bounds and introduces GP-MI, which improves them further and performs well in experiments.

paragraphs: In an asymmetric network, the relationship from one node to another can differ from the relationship in the reverse direction. The paper develops hierarchical quasi-clustering to preserve this directionality in the output. Its goal is a hierarchy that retains information carried by the asymmetry of the original network.

The authors show that the resulting output structure is equivalent to a finite quasi-ultrametric space. This mathematical representation lets them study which methods satisfy two desirable properties. Under those admissibility requirements, they prove that a modified form of single linkage is the only qualifying quasi-clustering method. The uniqueness claim is therefore tied to the stated framework and properties.

The paper also proves stability and establishes invariance properties of the proposed method, strengthening its theoretical characterization beyond admissibility alone. Algorithms make the construction usable, and a study of migration within the United States illustrates its value. That application provides a setting where preserving the direction of relationships is integral to the analysis.
icml-2014-hierarchical-quasi-clustering-.tldr: Hierarchical quasi-clustering preserves network directionality, with modified single linkage uniquely satisfying the paper's two admissibility properties.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems often face rapidly changing inventories, making contextual bandits a natural way to learn as recommendations are served. Evaluating a new learning algorithm directly on users can risk revenue. The paper addresses the resulting need to estimate performance offline using previously collected data.

Existing data-driven evaluation methods can reject most of those historical observations, leaving only a small fraction available for estimation. The authors identify this loss of usable information as a major source of poor accuracy. They propose a bootstrap-based method that improves estimation accuracy and also provides a measure of the estimate's quality.

That second output matters because deployment decisions depend on how much confidence to place in an offline result. The paper presents theoretical and experimental evidence of superiority over the state-of-the-art methods considered, along with an analysis of convergence for the quality measure. Its contribution is therefore both a better performance estimate and additional information for assessing the risk of first deploying a recommender.
icml-2014-improving-offline-evaluation-o.tldr: A bootstrap-based method improves offline contextual-bandit evaluation and supplies a measure of estimation quality to inform deployment decisions.

paragraphs: The paper asks which users in one social network are likely to join another. Cross-domain classifiers can approach this prediction problem, but differences between networks can make transferred knowledge unreliable. Even users present in both networks may behave differently across them, complicating their role as a bridge.

The proposed approach identifies common users whose behavior is consistent across the two networks. A method called Consistent Incidence Co-Factorization finds these users. Domain-UnBiased classifiers then transfer knowledge only through that selected group, making behavioral consistency the criterion for deciding which shared users should support cross-network prediction.

This design directly addresses heterogeneity between the source and target networks. Shared membership provides potential connections, while consistent behavior determines which connections the method uses. Extensive experiments show that the approach handles heterogeneity and improves prediction accuracy. The findings support selective transfer based on user behavior as a useful strategy for the target-node prediction problem studied.
icml-2014-learning-the-consistent-behavi.tldr: The method improves cross-network user prediction by transferring knowledge through shared users whose behavior remains consistent across networks.

paragraphs: Learning the parameters of a Markov random field requires estimating relationships represented by its graph. This paper introduces an algorithm that distributes this work over the graph's cliques, the groups of mutually connected variables. It is designed to be efficient for a large class of practical models.

The algorithm is embarrassingly parallel: its learning tasks naturally separate by clique and can be carried out in parallel. For graphs of bounded degree, the authors establish complexity that grows linearly with the number of cliques. That condition is part of the scaling result, linking the computational claim to the graph's connectivity.

For log-linear models, the method also needs only local sufficient statistics to estimate parameters. These statistics summarize the relevant local information in the observations, reducing the data each estimation task needs. The contribution combines computational separation with a local data requirement. Together, these properties explain why the approach is suited to parallel parameter learning in the model classes described.
icml-2014-linear-and-parallel-learning-o.tldr: Clique-wise parallel learning gives linear complexity for bounded-degree Markov random fields and uses only local sufficient statistics for log-linear models.

paragraphs: Structured prediction with hidden variables involves uncertainty about parts of the model that are not directly observed. The paper proposes the marginal structured SVM, or MSSVM, to account for that uncertainty. Its central claim is that handling hidden-variable uncertainty properly can improve predictions, particularly when that uncertainty is large.

The method also produces a smoother objective function. The authors report that this allows gradient-based optimization to converge significantly faster than for latent structured SVMs. Thus, the proposed treatment of hidden variables affects both the model's predictions and the computational behavior of the procedure used to fit it.

The paper reports that MSSVM can significantly outperform latent structured SVMs and other leading methods, and consistently outperforms hidden conditional random fields on the simulated and real datasets studied. It also introduces a unified framework containing MSSVM and several existing methods as special cases. This framework helps relate their modeling choices and interpret practical comparisons among them.
icml-2014-marginal-structured-svm-with-h.tldr: Marginal structured SVMs account for hidden-variable uncertainty, with reported gains in prediction and faster gradient-based optimization.

paragraphs: Multi-label classification becomes challenging when the output contains many possible classes. Label-space dimension reduction addresses this by representing labels in a smaller latent space and decoding predictions back into the original space. The paper develops FaIE, a method that makes this compact representation sensitive to the available input features.

FaIE directly learns a code matrix and a linear decoding matrix without assuming a particular encoding process. Its objective jointly favors two properties: recovering the original labels from the codes and predicting those codes from the features. This balances what the representation preserves about the outputs with how readily a predictor can infer it.

The method can also be specified to learn an explicit encoding function. A kernel extension handles nonlinear relationships between the feature space and the latent representation. Extensive benchmark experiments demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The main contribution is a formulation in which label compression and feature-based predictability are optimized together, shaping the latent space around both tasks.
icml-2014-multi-label-classification-via.tldr: FaIE learns compact label representations that jointly support accurate label reconstruction and prediction from input features.

paragraphs: The paper studies repeated routing decisions by selfish players in a non-atomic game, where individual players have negligible influence on overall traffic. Players choose routes using regret-minimizing learning algorithms. The question is whether the resulting population behavior approaches the set of Nash equilibria as learning continues.

Previously known no-regret guarantees establish convergence for a subsequence of population strategies. That leaves open what happens along the complete sequence of decisions. The authors focus on this stronger requirement: whether the actual sequence converges to the equilibrium set, rather than only selected points along the learning process.

They prove full-sequence convergence for a large class of online learning algorithms inspired by continuous-time replicator dynamics. They also prove that discounted Hedge belongs to this class, establishing its convergence in the studied routing setting. The result connects a concrete learning algorithm to stable long-run population behavior while keeping the guarantee specific to the algorithm class and game model analyzed.
icml-2014-on-the-convergence-of-no-regre.tldr: A broad class of no-regret algorithms, including discounted Hedge, has full-sequence convergence to Nash equilibria in repeated non-atomic routing.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to select K high-reward options from N stochastic bandit arms. It evaluates a selected set through aggregate regret: the difference between its average expected reward and that of the optimal set. This focuses attention on the quality of the selected group, a criterion motivated in part by crowdsourcing.

The authors propose a probably approximately correct algorithm. With probability at least 1−δ, it returns K arms whose aggregate regret is at most ε. The guarantee therefore allows a controlled reward shortfall and a controlled probability of failure, expressing the selection goal in terms of the chosen performance measure.

They establish a sample-complexity upper bound and a matching lower bound, showing optimal sample requirements under the formulation studied. Experiments on synthetic and real data report superior performance for the proposed algorithm. The contribution combines a group-level measure of selection quality, a high-probability guarantee, and evidence that the resulting procedure is useful beyond its theoretical analysis.
icml-2014-optimal-pac-multiple-arm-ident.tldr: The paper gives a sample-optimal PAC algorithm for selecting K bandit arms whose average expected reward is close to optimal.

paragraphs: A lifelong reinforcement-learning agent should be able to use earlier experience to learn later tasks more efficiently. Options provide one way to retain that experience: they are subpolicies that act over multiple steps. The paper investigates when these extended actions can reduce the amount of experience needed for learning.

The authors provide a formal analysis of the sample complexity of reinforcement learning with options, describing it as the first such analysis. This gives a theoretical basis for interpreting earlier empirical observations about when and how options accelerate learning. The analysis also quantifies the benefit options can provide across a lifelong learning setting.

These results motivate a new option-discovery algorithm whose objective is to minimize overall sample complexity across tasks. This connects the choice of reusable behaviors to the total learning effort of the agent. The contribution is both an analysis of the potential value of options and an algorithm designed around that analysis; acceleration remains a benefit that options may provide.
icml-2014-pac-inspired-option-discovery-.tldr: A sample-complexity analysis explains how options can accelerate lifelong reinforcement learning and motivates an option-discovery algorithm.

paragraphs: Parallel inference promises to distribute computational work across multiple processing nodes. The paper examines a previously proposed reparameterization of the Dirichlet process intended to enable non-approximate parallel MCMC inference. Although that approach had been adopted in several fields, the authors argue that its distribution of work makes it impractical.

The central problem is extreme imbalance in how data are allocated across nodes. The paper characterizes requirements for efficient parallel inference and shows that the examined method fails most of them, while approximate approaches often satisfy most. Both theoretical and experimental analyses support the load-balancing criticism.

The authors further show that the analyzed load balance is independent of dataset size and the number of available nodes. Consequently, increasing those quantities does not resolve the identified imbalance. The paper closes by suggesting other research directions for efficient non-approximate inference. Its finding concerns the practical shortcomings of the studied approach, rather than establishing that efficient exact parallel inference is impossible.
icml-2014-pitfalls-in-the-use-of-paralle.tldr: The paper shows that a proposed exact parallel Dirichlet-process inference scheme suffers from severe load imbalance that additional data or nodes do not fix.

paragraphs: Rectangular partitions provide a way to organize matrices used in relational data analysis. Such partitions can follow a regular grid, a hierarchy, or an arbitrary arrangement. The paper focuses on arbitrary arrangements, for which existing probabilistic models were sufficiently complicated to make their statistical behavior difficult to analyze.

The authors introduce the rectangular tiling process as a probabilistic model for this setting. It represents arbitrary rectangular partitioning of an infinite-dimensional matrix through a conditional projective limit. The construction rests on projective systems and infinite extensions of conditional probabilities, giving the proposed process an explicit mathematical foundation.

Its ability to represent partitions involving infinitely many elements places it alongside the kinds of constructions used in Bayesian nonparametric modeling. The contribution is a new foundation for modeling arbitrary rectangular organization in relational data. By addressing a setting whose existing models hindered statistical analysis, it expands the available mathematical framework beyond regular-grid and hierarchical partition models.
icml-2014-rectangular-tiling-process-ad8.tldr: The rectangular tiling process gives a mathematically grounded probabilistic model for arbitrary rectangular partitions of infinite-dimensional matrices.

paragraphs: Sparse learning often produces models in which many feature coefficients are zero. Safe screening accelerates fitting by eliminating features guaranteed to have zero coefficients at a specified regularization value. This is especially useful with many features or when fitting several regularization settings to choose a model.

The paper introduces Sasvi, which derives screening rules from a variational inequality expressing necessary and sufficient optimality conditions for the dual problem. Several existing Lasso screening approaches can be viewed as relaxations of Sasvi. This relationship establishes a stronger safe screening rule while retaining the guarantee that removed features have zero coefficients.

The authors also analyze monotonicity properties of Sasvi for Lasso. These properties allow them to identify a sure-removal regularization parameter for each feature, connecting screening decisions across regularization choices. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The contribution is a tighter mathematical basis for reducing the optimization problem before spending computation on features that cannot contribute.
icml-2014-safe-screening-with-variationa.tldr: Sasvi uses dual optimality conditions to derive stronger safe Lasso screening rules and identify feature-specific sure-removal regularization parameters.

paragraphs: GPstruct uses a Gaussian process prior over energy functions relating inputs to structured outputs. It combines kernel methods, nonparametric modeling, and Bayesian inference, but its memory use grows quadratically and training time cubically with the number of latent variables. These costs obstruct applications involving large grid factor graphs.

The paper develops an ensemble approach to make learning more scalable. Individual predictors train on subsets of latent variables and bootstrap samples of the data. These smaller training tasks can be distributed, providing a way to apply the model to image segmentation problems with far more latent variables.

Experiments include an image-segmentation setting with four million latent variables. The method outperforms widely used conditional random fields trained with pseudo-likelihood and improves on recent marginal-optimization methods in both prediction and uncertainty calibration. It also generalizes well across the training-set sizes evaluated. These findings support the ensemble approach as a practical route to larger GPstruct applications while preserving useful predictive uncertainty.
icml-2014-scalable-gaussian-process-stru.tldr: An ensemble of smaller GPstruct predictors scales structured Gaussian-process learning to millions of latent variables and improves segmentation results.

paragraphs: Robust Markov decision processes handle uncertainty about model parameters through a minimax planning approach. Dynamic programming can solve smaller instances, but the number of states and decisions in realistic problems can make direct computation prohibitive. The paper tackles this scaling problem while retaining the robust treatment of uncertainty.

The authors develop an approximate dynamic programming method using ideas from reinforcement learning and function approximation. Its mathematical basis is a projected fixed-point equation. This provides an approximation-based route to solving large robust planning problems, replacing the need to handle the full problem through the smaller-scale dynamic programming methods discussed.

The method is proved to succeed under certain technical conditions, so the guarantee is conditional on those requirements. A simulation involving option pricing demonstrates its effectiveness in the application studied. The paper's contribution is a way to extend robust MDP planning toward larger settings, together with theoretical support for the approximation and an illustrative simulation of its use.
icml-2014-scaling-up-robust-mdps-using-f.tldr: Function approximation extends robust MDP planning to larger problems, with conditional theoretical guarantees and an option-pricing simulation.

paragraphs: Pooling constructs a representation by applying a redundant linear transform, a pointwise nonlinearity, and local aggregation. Such representations help recognition by contracting nearby inputs, but their usefulness also depends on retaining stable information. The paper asks when a signal can be recovered from its pooled representation.

The authors calculate upper and lower Lipschitz bounds for pooling based on the ℓ₁, ℓ₂, and ℓ∞ norms, together with half-rectified versions. These bounds describe how changes in the input relate to changes in the representation. They provide sufficient conditions for designing invertible pooling layers, with the lower bound controlling the regularity of the inverse.

Numerical experiments on MNIST and image patches confirm that phase-recovery algorithms can invert the pooling layers studied. Nearest-neighbor regression also empirically verifies the role of the lower Lipschitz constant in inverse regularity. The results connect pooling design to both recoverability and stability, showing how contraction can coexist with recoverable information under suitable conditions.
icml-2014-signal-recovery-from-pooling-r.tldr: Lipschitz bounds give sufficient conditions for invertible pooling layers, with experiments demonstrating signal recovery and inverse stability.

paragraphs: Planted graph models generate edges according to hidden cluster memberships, and the recovery task is to infer those clusters from the graph. This paper studies the high-dimensional setting, where the number of clusters can grow with the number of nodes. It separates the availability of enough information from the computational effort needed to use it.

The authors identify four parameter regions. Recovery is impossible in the first. In the hard region, an exponential-time maximum likelihood estimator succeeds, while no polynomial-time method is known. In the easy region, a polynomial-time convexified estimator succeeds. In the simple region, counting or thresholding suffices. The analyzed algorithms also provably fail in the harder regions preceding their successful ones.

The results establish minimax recovery guarantees and extend to submatrix localization, also called biclustering. They expose a progression from statistical impossibility to increasingly inexpensive recovery. Crucially, the hard region describes a gap in known efficient methods; the statement that none is known does not establish impossibility for every polynomial-time algorithm.
icml-2014-statistical-computational-phas.tldr: The paper separates planted-cluster recovery into four regimes, revealing how statistical feasibility and computational requirements change with model parameters.

paragraphs: Large, fully observed binary matrices occur in many applications, and probabilistic matrix factorization offers a way to model them. Batch inference can be costly because it processes the entire matrix before updating model parameters. The paper develops stochastic inference to make useful progress without waiting for each complete pass.

The proposed algorithm includes new strategies for subsampling the data, which produce substantial gains over standard uniform sampling. This makes the choice of observations within an update an important part of the method. The authors also derive an algorithm that adjusts minibatch size online, automatically controlling how much data each update uses.

The method exhibits faster convergence rates than more expensive batch approaches and better predictive performance than scalable alternatives. These findings connect computational efficiency with the quality of the resulting model. The contribution combines stochastic updates, improved sampling, and adaptive minibatch selection for the specific setting of fully observed binary matrices, addressing several decisions that determine the effectiveness of scalable inference.
icml-2014-stochastic-inference-for-scala.tldr: Stochastic matrix-factorization inference combines improved subsampling with adaptive minibatch sizes to model fully observed binary matrices more efficiently.

paragraphs: Metric learning determines how distances between examples should be measured. This paper proposes a two-stage construction that first represents each example as a probability distribution. The distribution is obtained by computing similarities between the example and a fixed collection of anchor points.

The second stage measures distance through the Fisher information geometry of those distributions. This induces a new family of distances in the original input space. The construction allows the geometry of probability distributions to determine how the original examples are separated, using the anchor-based representation as the connection between the two spaces.

Unlike kernelized metric learning, the method does not require its similarity measure to be positive semidefinite. The authors also interpret it as a local metric-learning method with a well-defined distance approximation. Evaluations on multiple datasets report significant improvements over other metric-learning methods and SVMs. The contribution combines flexibility in the initial similarity measure with a principled geometric definition of the resulting distance.
icml-2014-two-stage-metric-learning-060a.tldr: A two-stage method turns anchor similarities into probability distributions and uses Fisher information geometry to define learned distances.
